arguments.why: Learners treat the larger denominator as meaning a larger fraction, so they think 1/8 is bigger than 1/4 because 8 is more than 4.
arguments.missingBasic: Understanding that the denominator shows how many equal parts the whole is split into
arguments.explanation: The denominator tells you how many equal parts the whole is cut into. More parts means each part is smaller, so 1/8 is smaller than 1/4.

reteach.title: Comparing unit fractions
reteach.youNeed: Fraction bars or paper strips cut into halves, quarters and eighths

steps.text: Show a whole strip and cut one into 4 equal parts and another into 8 equal parts. Point out that cutting into more pieces makes each piece smaller.
Hold up 1/4 and 1/8 side by side. Ask which is bigger. Let learners see that 1/4 covers more of the strip than 1/8.
Practise with more pairs: 1/2 vs 1/3, 1/3 vs 1/6, 1/5 vs 1/10. Always compare by looking at the size of the pieces, not the denominator number.

structuredContent.title: Class Test 1: Fractions and decimals
topicNames: Adding fractions with the same denominator

arguments.why: Learners add the numerators and denominators as if they were whole numbers, so they think 1/2 + 1/4 equals 2/6.
arguments.missingBasic: Understanding that fractions need the same denominator (same-sized parts) before they can be added
arguments.explanation: To add fractions with different denominators, first change them so they have the same denominator. Then add only the top numbers and keep the bottom number the same.

reteach.title: Adding fractions with different denominators
reteach.youNeed: Fraction bars or paper strips, chalkboard or paper

steps.text: Show that 1/2 and 1/4 are different-sized pieces. Use fraction bars to show that 1/2 is the same as 2/4.
Work through 1/2 + 1/4 together: change 1/2 to 2/4, then add 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. Emphasise that only the top numbers are added, the bottom stays the same.
Practise with 2/3 + 1/6 and 1 1/2 + 2 1/4, changing to the same denominator first before adding.
